origin_region: Shandong · Pingyin (Pingyin rose) and Gansu · Yongdeng (Kushui rose); damask rosebuds also come from Iran, Bulgaria and Pakistan
cultivar: Rosa rugosa types for Chinese meigui (the Kushui rose is a rugosa hybrid); Rosa × damascena for Middle Eastern rosebuds
processing: Tight buds are picked at dawn just before they open, when the scent is strongest, and dried at low temperature in shade or warm-air dryers; better lots are dried without sulfur fumigation, which is sometimes used to keep the colour.
harvest_season: A short flush in May and June, picked over two or three weeks; the whole year's supply is dried then.
appearance_dry: Small, tight buds one to two centimetres long, pink to deep purple-red with a green calyx and a little loose petal.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow with a pink blush, clear.
appearance_wet: The buds swell and loosen into soft, faded petals with a strong sweet-rose scent.
taste_profile: Delicate rose perfume with a honeyed sweetness and a faint tannic grip from the calyx; soft and gentle, never heavy, unless far too many buds go in.

brewing.notes: 5–8 buds per cup, water at 80–90 °C, 4 minutes; boiling water turns the scent soapy. The same buds take a second steep. A few buds added to black tea, white tea or ripe pu-erh is the more common use in China.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's May–June harvest and best within a year, because the colour fades from deep pink to brown and the scent goes with it; Chinese sellers usually state the harvest year, the origin (Pingyin and Kushui are the names to look for) and the grade, with large, uniform, deep-coloured buds at the top. 'Sulfur-free' is a meaningful claim: fumigated buds look unnaturally bright and smell faintly sharp. Rose petals (loose, no calyx) are a separate, cheaper product used for blending.
description:
Rose bud tea is dried rosebuds, nothing else: a handful in a glass, hot water, and a pale pink-gold cup that smells exactly like a rose garden in June. In China it is a women's tea by tradition and a common addition to black tea and ripe pu-erh; in Iran, Turkey and the Gulf, damask rosebuds are brewed the same way and used in blends.

The buds are picked before they open, at dawn, and dried gently; what you are buying is scent, and scent is fragile. Chinese meigui roses are rugosa types grown for exactly this purpose, with Pingyin in Shandong and the Kushui rose of Gansu the famous origins, and the buds are graded by size, colour and intactness. Damask rosebuds from Iran or Bulgaria are smaller, paler and slightly more perfumed.

The cup is soft and sweet with a clean rose aroma and a little grip from the green calyx; it is easy to overdo, and ten buds in a small cup tastes of soap. Water under the boil and four minutes is right, and the buds take a second steep. In a pot of black tea, three or four buds make a rose black tea; in ripe pu-erh they cut the earthiness; in white tea they are lovely cold-brewed.

Buy the current year's buds, deep pink to purple-red rather than brown, from a seller who states the harvest and the origin, and prefer sulfur-free lots. Loose rose petals without the calyx are a different product, cheaper and meant for blending.

It has traditionally been drunk as a gentle, warming everyday tea; whatever you make of that, it is a pretty, inexpensive infusion and the easiest way into scented teas. Try a few buds in a glass of Keemun black tea next.
